📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that moving out of your parents’ house costs more than the rent, so price the whole first year before you commit. Count the cash it takes to move in, add up a month of rent and bills, and check that total against your take-home pay. Then save one to three months of that total before you sign a lease.

Moving in can cost several thousand dollars, most of it due before you get the keys.

Sources indicate that most landlords want the first month’s rent and a security deposit that’s often the same amount, and some ask for the last month’s rent too. The Federal Trade Commission says a utility can ask a new customer for a deposit as well. Ask whether the utility will take a letter of guarantee from a parent instead, a written promise to cover your bill if you fall behind.

Furniture, kitchen basics, and the move itself add to that. Take every hand-me-down your family offers, buy the rest secondhand, and line up friends with a truck before you pay for movers.

Next, price a normal month: rent, utilities, internet, renters insurance, groceries, getting to work, and your phone if you’re coming off a family proposal. Check that total against your take-home pay, the amount that reaches your account after taxes and deductions, not your salary.

Say you take home $3,200 a month, rent is $1,050, and the other bills come to $950, so a month costs $2,000 and leaves $1,200 for loan payments, savings, and everything else. Moving in takes about $3,500, which covers the first month’s rent, a deposit of the same amount, $200 to set up utilities, $900 for secondhand furniture and kitchen gear, and $300 for the move. A three-month cushion adds $6,000, so the goal is about $9,500 saved before you sign.

Industry observers note that the cushion covers a car repair or a gap between jobs, so neither goes on a credit card. Make it at least a month of rent and bills, and three if your hours or pay vary. If the numbers don’t work yet, a roommate or a cheaper area lowers your rent, and the deposit and cushion you need fall with it.

According to recent reports, work out your own target before you tour a single apartment. Then pay yourself first until you reach it. Move part of every paycheck into savings the day it arrives, before you spend on anything else.

Keep that money in one of the best high-yield savings accounts so it earns interest until you sign.

A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

In a recent development, when Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pitch venture capital firms only if your business could grow fast enough to sell or go public for many times what investors pay, since a fund needs a few winners like that to cover its many losses. If yours will grow steadily instead, fund it with savings or a loan and keep the whole firm.

Of U.S. startups that raised early-stage venture capital from 1985 to 2009, about 55% ended at a loss for their investors, Harvard Business School researchers found. The 6% that returned more than five times the money brought in about half of everything investors got back.

So a venture firm looks for companies that could join that 6%, with a large market, fast-growing sales, and a realistic path to being sold or going public. A business that will earn its owner a good living but never sell for many times what investors would pay fails that test, however well it’s run.

According to recent reports, the money is expensive. A typical seed round, one of a startup’s first rounds of outside money, sells close to a fifth of the firm, and so does the larger Series A round that follows, Carta’s 2026 benchmarks show. Investors also get preferred stock, which usually repays them before your shares get anything when the company is sold, and they often take a seat on your board. Venture funds typically run at least 10 years and then cash out, the SEC notes, so expect pressure to grow fast enough to sell or go public before then.

If you fit, skip the cold email. In a survey of 885 venture capitalists published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, only 10% of their deals came from founders who reached out on their own. The median firm surveyed considered 100 deals for every one it closed. A software founder whose subscriptions grow every month pitches only firms that back early software companies, gets introduced by a founder one of them funded, and raises a $3 million seed round for 20% of her company.

A restaurant owner turned down by every venture firm she pitches opens a second location with a bank loan the Small Business Administration guarantees instead and keeps 100% of the business.

To fund a business like hers, compare the best small business loans.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, with all your savings in one account, a $9,000 balance looks like room for a vacation, even when $6,000 of it is your emergency fund.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Give each goal you’re saving for its own high-yield savings account or a named bucket inside one. That usually means one for yearly costs and one for your next major purchase, with your emergency fund in an account by itself. Separate balances show what each dollar is for, so you won’t spend one goal’s money on another by mistake.

In a recent development, with all your savings in one account, a $9,000 balance looks like room for a vacation, even when $6,000 of it is your emergency fund. Nothing in your banking app says which dollars are already spoken for.

A goal needs its own account once it has a price and a date in the next few years, such as a car next year or a vacation next summer. A separate balance then reveals exactly how much of the price you’ve saved. Yearly costs like insurance premiums and holiday gifts can share one account, or each can get its own bucket as a sinking fund, money saved for that one cost.

The emergency fund stays apart because it’s the one balance that must be there in full when something goes wrong, and it belongs at a different bank from your checking.

It has been revealed that more accounts stop helping once one would charge a monthly fee or require a minimum balance, or once you’d have more balances than you’ll check each month. Skip an account for any goal you aren’t saving toward yet.

Open the goal accounts at one high-yield savings bank that lets you add them free. Capital One lets you open a separate 360 Performance Savings account for each goal, with no monthly fee or minimum balance. Ally Bank lets you split one savings account into buckets, named sections of the same balance.

Recent findings suggest that nickname each account for its goal and give it an automatic transfer on payday, or split one transfer among your buckets. The $9,000 then becomes a $6,000 emergency fund, $1,800 for insurance premiums and holiday gifts, and $1,200 toward a vacation, so the vacation account indicates $1,200 to spend, not $9,000.

When the vacation is paid for, rename its account for your next goal instead of opening another.

The shopping that pays is shopping for someone else, as a grocery shopper on a delivery app, a personal shopper, or a mystery shopper, since cash back on your own purchases only lowers what you spend. Before you count an app’s payouts as income, subtract what your miles cost and the self-employment tax you’ll owe.

A shopper app lets you pick your orders and hours around a day job, and it reveals each order’s pay before you accept it.

Instacart pays per batch, its name for a job, based on the driving distance, item count, and expected shopping time, plus promotions when demand runs high and 100% of the tip. Shipt pays per order based on its own estimate of the time and effort, at least $16 an hour by that estimate, plus bonuses and tips. Taking longer than the estimate earns nothing extra. Both require a reliable car and treat you as an independent contractor, so no tax comes out of your pay.

According to recent reports, price each mile at the IRS’s standard mileage rate, which is also what you can deduct for each business mile. The IRS bases it on what it costs to own and run a car, not just gas. At an illustrative 75 cents a mile, an hour of work that pays $25 and takes 20 miles of driving leaves $10 after the car. Self-employment tax, due once your year’s profit reaches $400, takes about 14% of that $10, so you keep roughly $8.60 before income tax. Over a full week, counting the hours you wait between orders, the same math gives your real hourly pay.

Instacart never penalizes you for passing on a batch, so you can skip any whose miles would cost most of what it pays. Log every mile you drive for work, since the deduction lowers your income tax and self-employment tax.

Before you accept any order or assignment, subtract its miles, priced at the IRS rate, from what it pays, then set aside about 14% of the rest for self-employment tax.

#56667. Needs vs. Wants – Ask What Would Suffer If You Cut the Expense

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (482 w)

Needs vs. Wants – Ask What Would Suffer If You Cut the Expense

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, to sort your budget into needs and wants, ask what would happen if each expense disappeared.
  • In a recent development, sorting this way reveals what you can cut without real harm.
  • Ask the question of every expense, and the needs come down to a short list: shelter, utilities, basic food, insurance, health care, the transportation and child care that let you work, and minimum debt payments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, to sort your budget into needs and wants, ask what would happen if each expense disappeared. If your health, safety, housing, or ability to earn would suffer, it’s a need. Everything else is a want, and so is whatever you pay above the basic version of a need.

In a recent development, sorting this way reveals what you can cut without real harm. It also settles a debate with a partner, or with yourself, over what’s essential, because the answer turns on what would suffer, not on how you feel about the bill.

Ask the question of every expense, and the needs come down to a short list: shelter, utilities, basic food, insurance, health care, the transportation and child care that let you work, and minimum debt payments. Those payments make the list because a missed one hurts your credit and often adds a late fee, and falling behind on a car loan or mortgage can cost you the car or the home.

Much of what you can cut sits inside those needs. A phone and a reliable car both pass the test, but the newest phone and a upcoming car are needs bought at a want’s price. The basic version is the need, and anything you pay above it is a want.

Say your phone bill covers unlimited data and the payment on a latest phone, for $95 a month, and a basic plan with enough data to stay reachable for work would cost $30. The $30 is a need, and the other $65 is a want. Food splits the same way, with groceries as the need and whatever takeout costs beyond the same meals cooked at home as the want.

Industry observers note that sort every charge on last month’s bank and card statements into needs and wants, splitting any that mix the two, then total each side. Compared with the 50/30/20 rule, the two totals show whether needs or wants are the reason your savings come up short.

When money gets tight, cut from the want side first, starting with whatever you’d miss least. Then trim each need to its basic version rather than dropping it. For the phone, that means switching to a cheap cell phone proposal and keeping the phone you have long after its last payment.

#56665. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2593 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
  • According to recent reports, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
  • This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

According to recent reports, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

In a recent development, is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

Industry observers note that to answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

It has been revealed that your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

In a recent development, but if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

According to recent reports, now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

But in that same time period, your share of organization earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

It has been revealed that so as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

Recent findings suggest that but Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual firm’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

According to recent reports, but what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more rapidly?

In a recent development, in the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 massive companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

There’s one common theme in the major tech organization boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

It has been revealed that but that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

It has been revealed that they may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

Sources indicate that while the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

Recent findings suggest that so What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

Sources indicate that as I noted earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

In a recent development, everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

According to recent reports, wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

According to recent reports, just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

According to recent reports, longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

What About Paying Off Your House?

Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

Industry observers note that if you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

In the Comments: what are your thoughts on the current stock market boom, future crashes and busts, and the role of Artificial Intelligence in our future?

Unlike a long-term rental, a vacation rental earns only on the nights guests book, while its mortgage, property tax, and insurance come due either way.

In a recent development, take a cabin that rents for $230 a night and costs $19,000 a year for its mortgage, property tax, insurance, utilities, and upkeep. Each booked night adds $40 for cleaning, supplies, and booking platform fees, and a manager takes 25% of revenue. At 70% occupancy, meaning guests book 70% of the year’s nights, the listing agent’s spreadsheet indicates the cabin earning about $15,000 a year after costs. If it books 85% of its summer weekends but, like similar cabins nearby, only 35% of the year, it loses about $2,000 a year.

Recent findings suggest that don’t count on that loss to cut your tax bill. When guests stay seven days or fewer on average, the IRS’s passive-loss rules don’t count the home as a rental activity. Its losses, depreciation included, then lower the tax on your salary only if you materially participate, such as working on it over 100 hours a year and no fewer hours than anyone else, including a manager.

Before you make an offer, take four steps:.

In a recent development, selling preorders on Kickstarter can pay for your first production run without a loan or giving up a share of your business. Backers pay only if you reach your goal, and then you owe each one the reward they pledged for. So set the goal at the full cost of making and shipping every reward, plus fees.

A campaign that misses its goal leaves you owing nothing, since no backer is charged and Kickstarter takes no fee. The risky campaign is the one that reaches a goal set too low.

Once a campaign is funded, Kickstarter’s terms require you to finish the project and deliver every reward as promised. If the rewards cost more to make and ship than the pledges bring in after fees, you pay the difference. Promise backers a delivery date with room for factory and shipping delays, too.

It has been revealed that add up what delivering every reward costs: your factory’s price for the smallest run it will make, packaging, and shipping to each backer, by country if you ship abroad. Then add Kickstarter’s 5% fee and payment processing, which on a U.S. project is 3% plus 30 cents for each pledge of $10 or more.

According to recent reports, say a board game designer’s printer quotes $14 a copy for 2,000 copies, and shipping averages $10 a backer. She sets a $30,000 goal and raises $41,000 from 900 backers. Fees take about $3,550 and shipping $9,000, together about 30% of what she raised. The $28,450 left pays for all 2,000 copies, with 1,100 to sell after the campaign.

In a recent development, to reach a goal that covers every reward, line up backers before you launch. Collect email addresses, then send people to your project’s Kickstarter pre-launch page, which emails its followers when you go live. Kickstarter says that, on average, 32% of the people who follow a pre-launch page go on to pledge, against 17% of those who follow after launch.

Kickstarter locks the goal at launch, so get your factory’s and shipper’s quotes in writing before you set it.

After the raise, you owe annual reports, filed there within 120 days of your fiscal year’s end and posted on your website, though they need no accountant’s review.

What you sell decides what you give up:.

You need that review to raise more than $124,000 and an audit above $618,000, though a first crowdfunding raise can use a review up to $1,235,000.

Say a neighborhood brewery raises $400,000 from 1,100 customers, most investing a few hundred dollars, to open a second taproom. On Wefunder it pays $31,600 and needs a review, not an audit. The SEC lets you test interest before you file if you say no money is being accepted and no one is committed, so poll your customers before you hire an accountant.

FDIC Insurance Covers $250,000 per Ownership Category – Not Everything Your Bank Sells

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that FDIC insurance covers your checking, savings, CDs, and other deposits at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per ownership category, such as single or joint accounts.
  • Sources indicate that A bank with the FDIC sign at its teller windows can still hold some of your money that the FDIC won’t cover.
  • Deposits are insured automatically, with nothing to apply for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that FDIC insurance covers your checking, savings, CDs, and other deposits at an insured bank, up to $250,000 per ownership category, such as single or joint accounts. It doesn’t cover stocks, mutual funds, annuities, or crypto, even when you buy them at the bank. Confirm your bank on the FDIC’s BankFind, then total each category in its EDIE estimator.

Sources indicate that A bank with the FDIC sign at its teller windows can still hold some of your money that the FDIC won’t cover. The branch that opens your savings account may also sell you an annuity, and a CD you open later can push your total past the limit.

Deposits are insured automatically, with nothing to apply for. But the FDIC doesn’t cover bonds, life insurance, or the contents of a safe deposit box. A money market deposit account counts as a deposit, while a money market fund, despite the similar name, is an investment with no FDIC coverage.

An ownership category is the way you own an account. The common ones are single accounts in your name alone, joint accounts, retirement accounts such as IRAs, and trust accounts, which include a savings account or CD naming a beneficiary to inherit it. Each category is insured on its own, but all your accounts in one category at one bank share one limit, whether they’re checking, savings, or CDs. Opening one at another branch of the same bank doesn’t change that.

It has been revealed that take a saver with two accounts at one bank, both in her name alone with no beneficiary. Her savings account holds $180,000, and her CD holds $90,000. Both are single accounts, so the FDIC adds them together, and her $270,000 is $20,000 over the limit. She could name a beneficiary on the CD, which would make it a trust account with its own limit, or move $20,000 to a different insured bank.

To check your own coverage, search the FDIC’s BankFind by your bank’s name or web address to confirm it’s insured. Then enter each account’s balance and owners in EDIE, the FDIC’s Electronic Deposit Insurance Estimator, which demonstrates what’s insured at that bank and any amount over the limit. For a money app that isn’t a bank, look up the bank behind it instead.

Leave room under each category’s limit for at least a year of interest, since interest counts toward the limit through the day a bank fails.

#56651. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 13 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2455 w)

How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 13 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well.
  • And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.
  • As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re presently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

Industry observers note that as I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”.

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:.

Industry observers note that A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country. They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a firm in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

In a recent development, tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

Recent findings suggest that on average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most crucial part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to proposal far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Industry observers note that sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.).

According to recent reports, and this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Can Tariffs Bring Us More Jobs?

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a major one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Industry observers note that because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some upcoming models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

Recent findings suggest that but in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

In a recent development, on top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This major picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

Sources indicate that but when he unveils larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

The basic theory goes like this:.

In a recent development, so right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

Sources indicate that but presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:.

How Substantial are the Tariffs Right Now?

According to recent reports, even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

It has been revealed that so in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

In a recent development, for now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re swiftly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The Dark Side and the Bright Side.

According to recent reports, the most crucial phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:.

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:.

Recent findings suggest that I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:.

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Sources indicate that just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

Epilogue: Is it Almost Over Already?

According to recent reports, I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in substantial losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:.

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

In a recent development, right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it demonstrates that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines.

In a recent development, decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

There are two solutions to this:.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or.

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

In a recent development, I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

Sources indicate that so as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Sources indicate that when the Federal Reserve raises rates, the variable rates on your credit card balances and home equity line of credit climb on their own, but your savings rate rises only if your bank raises it. Put extra payments toward those balances first, and move the cash you’re saving to a high-yield savings account that passes the increase on.

The Fed raised its benchmark rate a quarter point in September, its first increase since July 2023.

In a recent development, A variable rate on a credit card or a home equity line of credit (HELOC) follows an index such as the prime rate, which moves with the Fed’s rate. Card issuers normally can’t raise the rate on a balance you already owe, but a rise in that index is one of the exceptions, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes. On a $10,000 card balance carried all year, each percentage point added to the rate costs about $100 in interest.

It has been revealed that online banks have passed more of each increase on to savers. During the 2022 and 2023 hikes, they raised deposit rates about 0.3 percentage point more than branch-based banks for each full point the Fed added, a National Bureau of Economic Research study found. At an online bank paying 4%, $20,000 earns about $800 a year. At a major bank paying 0.01%, it earns $2.

In a recent development, pay down card balances first, then a HELOC ahead of any fixed-rate loan charging the same rate or less. A card balance you’ll carry for months can move to a fixed-rate personal loan, or to a 0% balance transfer card you can pay off before the 0% period ends, after you compare the fees. If you’ll borrow for a car or a home soon, lock in a fixed rate before you buy.

Keep your emergency fund in a high-yield savings account. For fresh certificates of deposit (CDs), stick to terms of a year or less until rates level off, or build a CD ladder so part of your money comes due every six months.

Cash beyond that fund belongs on any card balance you carry. Banks charged an average 22.36% on cards carrying a balance in the third quarter, the Federal Reserve reports, more than five times what a 4% savings account pays.

The cocktail bar, the à la carte dining, the spa treatments available before departure — this is the part that makes the ChooseFI community members shake their heads in disbelief when they first experience it. Then you board and settle into Virgin's short-haul business class: a proper dedicated seat, a full meal service, attentive cabin crew. For a two-and-a-half-hour flight, it's a genuinely elevated experience.

You land in Athens refreshed, fed, and without having spent thousands of dollars. That's the positioning flight done right — and it's what separates travelers who understand the travel rewards system from those who are still paying cash for European business class.

Industry observers note that do this: Use it as a positioning flight on a broader trip This redemption was practically designed for trip architecture. If you're already planning a transatlantic journey — coming into London on a long-haul award — the 17,500-mile European hop becomes the natural, high-value conclusion. You're not just booking a short flight; you're completing a fully points-funded journey across two continents. Think of this as the last domino.

Industry observers note that do this: Compare cash prices before transferring Not all dates are created equal. A Tuesday in November to Rome might retail for $800 in business class — still a reasonable 4.6 CPP — while the same route on a Friday in July might hit $2,800, delivering 17+ CPP. Run the cash price check on Google Flights before you commit your miles. Target the high-cash-price windows for maximum value extraction.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming availability This is the single most common mistake. Transferring miles to Virgin Atlantic is a one-way street. Keep Flying Club active by earning miles through their shopping portal or partners, and wait for the right route and cash price moment to pounce.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The flight itself is short, but the value extends beyond the seat. #56641. SBA Loans Cost Less Than Online Business Loans – If You Can Wait Weeks

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (502 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

SBA Loans Cost Less Than Online Business Loans – If You Can Wait Weeks

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Choose an SBA loan over an online loan if you can wait weeks.
  • Owners turn to online lenders for speed.
  • Small Business Administration guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans, which banks and other approved lenders make.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Choose an SBA loan over an online loan if you can wait weeks. The SBA’s guarantee comes with a capped rate and terms up to 10 years for most uses, 25 for real estate. Expect to pledge collateral on loans over $50,000, sign a personal guarantee, and, as a startup, put in at least 10% of the cost.

Owners turn to online lenders for speed. In the Federal Reserve’s 2025 Small Business Credit Survey, 60% of firms that borrowed from online lenders mentioned their borrowing costs ran higher than expected, against 32% of large-bank borrowers.

An SBA loan is slower and cheaper. The U.S. Small Business Administration guarantees up to 85% of most 7(a) loans, which banks and other approved lenders make. In return for that backing, SBA rules cap a variable rate at the banks’ benchmark prime rate, now 7.00%, plus 3 to 6.5 percentage points, depending on the loan’s size.

Say a landscaper owes $120,000 on online term loans repaid over two years at 30% interest, about $6,710 a month. A 10-year 7(a) loan at a fixed 11% cuts that to about $1,650. The longer term costs more interest in total, about $78,000 over 10 years against $41,000 on the online loans. Extra payments shrink that, and a 7(a) loan shorter than 15 years carries no prepayment fee.

A 7(a) loan of up to $5 million can cover working capital, equipment, real estate, debt refinancing, or starting or buying a business. A 504 loan, made through a nonprofit Certified Development Tech giant, finances buildings, land, and long-lived machinery at a fixed rate. SBA microloans of up to $50,000 come from nonprofit lenders.

Under the SBA’s lending rules, every owner of 20% or more personally guarantees the whole loan, and a loan over $50,000 needs collateral, though a lender can’t refuse you for weak collateral alone. A business open a year or less must put in at least 10% of the total cost, and so must most buyers of a business.

To get an SBA loan, start with a bank that knows your business, and ask whether it’s an SBA Preferred Lender, one allowed to approve loans without the SBA’s review, which can take up to 10 business days. Or describe your needs in the SBA’s Lender Match tool, which lists interested lenders two business days later.

Apply once you know a substantial cost is coming, and keep online loans for needs that can’t wait weeks.

Compare the best small business loans and SBA lenders to choose where to apply.

Recent findings suggest that buy your next rental where rent is high against home prices. In 15 Midwest and Southern metros, a typical house rents for 7.4% to 11.2% of its value a year. Before you offer, check the city’s taxes, insurance, and vacancy, and what houses on that street actually rent for.

That share, a year’s rent divided by the price, is the gross yield, and it decides whether rent can cover a mortgage. In Zillow’s October 2026 figures, a typical house in the San Diego area rents for about 5% of its value a year, while one in the McAllen, Texas, area rents for 11.2%.

Now figure the mortgage payment on each, with 25% down and a 30-year loan at 7%. A typical McAllen-area house, worth $189,000, rents for about $1,760 a month, roughly $820 more than its $943 payment. A typical San Diego-area house, worth about $1 million, rents for about $4,130, about $860 short of its payment of nearly $5,000.

In a recent development, at those terms, the typical rent is higher than the mortgage payment in all 15 metros below, by about $270 a month in Little Rock up to about $820 in McAllen. That margin still has to pay the property taxes and insurance, plus the repairs, empty months, and management every landlord budgets for, so those costs decide whether a house makes money.

In a recent development, since October 2023, typical rents have risen faster than typical home prices, so the yield on a typical U.S. house has climbed from 7.0% to 7.4%.

Industry observers note that each price, rent, and yield here covers a whole metro area and uses Zillow’s typical single-family home value and rent, the middle of each market. Every metro on the list passed six tests:.

It has been revealed that two massive Texas metros fell short. San Antonio’s typical rent rose only 0.7% over the past year, and Census’s metro estimates put Dallas’s rental vacancy at 14.7% this summer, nearly twice the national rate.

Here they are, from the highest yield down, with each metro’s typical house value and monthly rent.

Recent findings suggest that property taxes come out of the rent every year, and several states on this list tax a rental more heavily than an owner’s home. Texas’s homestead exemptions, which shield part of a home’s value from tax, go only to an owner’s main home, so a rental in McAllen or El Paso is taxed on its full value, the state comptroller explains. Michigan charges a rental up to 18 mills, or $18 per $1,000 of taxable value, in school operating taxes that an owner’s home skips, according to its Treasury Department.

In South Carolina, a rental is assessed at 6% of its value, against 4% for an owner’s home, and pays school operating taxes the owner’s home skips, as Richland County, home to Columbia, explains. Indiana caps a rental’s yearly property tax at 2% of its assessed value, against 1% for an owner’s home, according to the state’s Department of Local Government Finance.

According to recent reports, insurance is the other major cost that varies by state. In Insurance.com’s 2026 study of quoted rates for a standard policy with $300,000 of coverage on the house, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Kansas averaged more than $5,000 a year, about twice the $2,872 national average. Texas averaged $4,582. Get a quote on a landlord policy for the exact house before you offer.

In a recent development, landlord law matters as well. Oregon, Washington, and California cap yearly rent increases statewide, while 36 states bar their cities from adopting rent control at all, according to the National Apartment Association, a landlords’ trade group.

Recent findings suggest that every number above describes a whole metro, which mixes blocks where houses rent swiftly with blocks where they sit empty. Before you offer, compare the rent the seller quotes with what similar houses nearby actually rent for. If you’re buying in another state, have a local agent or property manager pull those rents for you.

Start with the two or three metros whose typical prices fit your budget, and run one real listing in each through the mortgage test above, using its own tax bill and insurance quote.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that look for small business grants close to home, from city and state economic development offices, utilities, corporations, and foundations.
  • A grant is the cheapest money a business can get, since you never repay it and no one takes a share of the company.
  • Small Business Administration “does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business,” according to its own grants page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that look for small business grants close to home, from city and state economic development offices, utilities, corporations, and foundations. The SBA gives no grants to start or expand a business, and federal grants for companies mostly fund research or exporting. Apply only where your business fits the grant’s purpose.

A grant is the cheapest money a business can get, since you never repay it and no one takes a share of the company.

The U.S. Small Business Administration “does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business,” according to its own grants page. The federal grants a company can win go mostly to research, through the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs, and to exporters.

So for a shop, a restaurant, or a service business, the grants worth chasing are local.

Take a bakery owner who searches the federal grant listings and finds research and export programs, nothing for a bakery. Her city’s economic development office runs a storefront program that pays back half the cost of exterior work, up to $10,000. She applies before hiring anyone, as the program requires, wins a grant, spends $16,000 on a newly introduced sign, awning, and lighting, and gets $8,000 back once the work is done.

Here’s where to look, starting close to home, with what each source pays for and who can apply.

Industry observers note that A real government grant never charges you a fee. The Federal Trade Commission claims no agency will reach out to demand that you pay for a grant, and it warns against paying any up-front fee.

It also warns against paying for a list of grants, since the complete list of federal grants on Grants.gov is free.

Check the sender, too. The SBA states it writes only from email addresses ending in @sba.gov, and that anyone claiming to be the agency from another address should be reported as fraud.

In a recent development, read what the grant pays for first, since many fund a single purpose. Philadelphia’s Storefront Improvement Program covers exterior work such as signs, awnings, lighting, and paint, and STEP money goes only to export activities the SBA approves.

According to recent reports, then check what you’d have to put in yourself. Philadelphia’s program pays back up to half the cost of approved work, so you cover at least half and pay the whole bill until the city reimburses you. USDA’s Value-Added Producer Grants require a dollar-for-dollar match.

It has been revealed that many grants also want a business that’s already running. STEP is for established small businesses, and the $25,000 Wells Fargo grants the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce offered in 2026 required two years in business.

In a recent development, the competition is steep. Boston’s storefront program notes it lacks the money to give a grant to every eligible business, and Hiring Our Heroes names five winners a round. Winning takes an application that answers the funder’s scoring criteria point by point.

Start with one call to your city’s economic development office, and ask which grants it’s funding this year, what each one pays for, and how much of the cost you’d have to cover.
